Glove Fight Between Sullivan and Tug Wilson.

NEW YORK, July 17th.—Before 7 o'clock this evening the vicinity of Madison Square Garden was a perfect ocean of humanity, gathered there attracted by the announcement that within the walls of the garden Sullivan, champion of America, and Tug Wilson, champion of England, would have a glove fight. In the center of the building was a 44-foot ring, five feet above the floor. At half past 7 at least 12,000 people were in the garden, and half an hour later the number had grown to 15,000 or 16,000. At about 8:15 Harry Hill appeared in the ring, accompanied by Harry Evans and Tommy Cook, two English boxers, who gave a rattling set-to of three rounds. Two local boxers then engaged the attention of the crowd for a few minutes. At 9:38 Wilson and Sullivan, the first accompanied by Arthur Chambers and George Holden, and the latter by Billy Madden and Joe Goss, appeared in the ring. The vast mass of people rose and cheered, and seemed wild with delight. Betting at this time stood $100 to $75 in favor of the American. Both men stripped the waist. Harry Hill was chosen referee. The conditions of the fight announced that there were four窒bury rules of three minutes each, one minute rest, and ten seconds, in case of a knock down, for the fallen man to get up. If Wilson should fight four rounds Sullivan engaged to pay him $1,000 and half the gate money. Wilson, holding $1,000 in his gloved hand, stepped to where $1,000 in his gloved hand, stepped to where Sullivan sat and offered to bet that amount that he would not be knocked out of time. Sullivan declined the offer, saying there was already enough money on the match. At 9:40 Harry Hill called time, Sullivan seemed to tower above his adversary. His body has the perfect frame of a fighter. He stood the punishment inflicted by Sullivan, and, although knocked down twenty-seven times, fought against hope and pummelled and hammered in every conceivable manner. He managed to stand out for the four rounds and won $1,000 and his share of gate money. He showed great cunning in each of the rounds.

Lynching in Kershaw.
CAMDEN, July 17. On last Wednesday night an attempt was made to commit a rape in the northern part of Keesbaw County. The cries of the victim attracted attention, pursuit was made, and circumstances pointed to a negro boy named David Cook, who lived nearby. He was arrested on Saturday morning and was committed to jail. While being conveyed to Camden, in charge of two deputies, and when about five and a half miles from Camden, a party of masked men emerged from the woods and took the prisoner from the custody of the constables. Up to a late hour to-day I had not been able to learn further particulars. I understand to-night, however, that the body of the prisoner was found to-day hanging from a tree several miles above the place where the prisoner was taken from custody. The prisoner acknowledged that he was guilty of the crime charged against him, and further stated that this was not the first case of the kind in which he had been engaged. There is no excitement manifested here concerning the matter, and very little interest is displayed by the people in the section where the tragedy occurred.

Doings of the Elements.
Chicago, June 26.—The cyclonic storm, which for the past few days has traversed and desolated this section, seemed to have followed no particular course, but to have dipped down here and there at points widely separated, as cities in Michigan and Nebraska, Dakota Territory and southern Indiana. While the ravages in Iowa have been most serious to life and property, the aggregate losses in other parts of the region are very heavy. Among the casualties which have not been already mentioned the following may be given, as indicating the general character and violence of the elements: At Osceola, Iowa, yesterday, Adam Miller and Wm. Lowe were killed by lightning. A severe rain and wind storm visited Albia yesterday evening, with accompaniment of thunder and lightning. Trees snapped off like pistols, and many pranks were played by the wind, but no loss of life is reported. The storm appeared like a cyclone. Trains are delayed in the direction of McGregor, Iowa, by disasters to tracks and bridges. Much damage was done on Saturday in the neighborhood of Sionx City and Malvern, in northwestern Iowa. Between Morrison and Round Grove, Illinois, 2600 feet of the Chicago & Northwestern track was washed away. The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy suffered even worse. West of Mendola, Nebraska, yesterday morning, a terrific storm gathered in Butler county, and swept southwest through Saunders, Lancaster, Cass, Elco and Nehama counties, doing the greatest damage in a belt 25 miles in width between Wahoo and Weston. Corn was badly beaten down in the southern part of Saunders county, and small grain was utterly ruined. Two houses were blown down. In Wahoo a two-story barn was carried fifty feet through the air. A herd of 125 ponies were swept by the storm eight miles southward, over fields and through wire fences. Not a pane of glass was left in the windows facing the west. The schoolhouse at Clear Creek was completely wrecked. One man was killed and five injured near Talmadge, on the Missionri Pacific, while seeking shelter under a freight car, which was hurled against them. Corn will be put back two or three weeks. Numbers of cattle were carried down stream and drowned near Lanesboro, Minnesota. Roads were stripped of bridges, and made inaccessible, and crops were damaged somewhat, hay most severely. One man was drowned in Uldapho, Minnesota, while rescuing stock from the floods. There was a tornado at Marysville, Kansas, yesterday morning, and one is also reported at Kerwin, Muncie, Indiana, got the last of the wind, damage of about $60,000 being inflicted. Geo. Hawkes's family were severely shocked by lightning, the little daughter remaining unconscious a long time. Great damage to wheat is feared. Roofs were blown off, and much other damage done. At Decatur, Indiana, the loss was $4000. Three people have been killed there by recent tornadoes. The loss in Indianapolis is said to be fifty thousand dollars. Telegraph and telephone wires are blown down. At Lafayette, Indiana, was a terrible waterspout, eight feet high, on Saturday night, which chased a train coming to the city for a considerable distance. It whirled rocks and immense trees along in its course, but spent its force before it caught the train. A severe rain rain storm did $10,000 damage to Chester township, Ohio. Stock and grain suffered. Innumerable smaller casualties occurred, but these sufficiently illustrate the storm.

Another Warrior Seeking Justice.

WASHINGTON, June 28.—The secretary of war has under consideration the case of Major-General G. K. Warren, now lieutenant-colonel of engineers, who was relieved from command of the fifth corps at the battle of Five Forks, Va., in 1865 by General Sheridan. Warren made several efforts to have the matter investigated, but without avail until 1879, when President Hayes appointed a committee of inquiry, Major-General Hancock as president. The committee completed their report a few months ago; and a record of the case was submitted to Judge Advocate General Swaim for review. The committee found that General Sheridan had not exceeded his authority, but that in one or two instances he had misjudged the conduct of General Warren. The judge advocate general is said to approve the general finding of the court. It is not a case requiring further action. The record in the case comprises over seven thousand pages of foolscap, the largest that ever passed through the bureau of military justice.

News from Frenchburg, Menifee County, Kentucky, reports another calamity occurring at that town. A heavy rain raised Beaver Creek and flooded the town, the water standing six to eight feet deep in the streets and houses. Three dwellings were swept away and six of the inmates drowned. The names of the drowned are Mrs. John Fox, Mrs. Bryne and her two grown daughters, and two Misses Watkins, the daughters of Preacher Watkins. The bodies of four of them have been recovered. The flood covered the entire valley and swept away all the fencing and crops. The postoffice at Frenchburg, with all letters and papers, was carried away and lost. The distress of the people is pitiable. The heavy rainfall extended for fifteen or twenty miles, and all the streams were swollen higher than ever before known. The track of the K. and S. A. Railroad, on Slate Creek was washed away in several places, and great destruction of property done. A woman on Slate Creek left her house with her child in her arms, but before she could reach the hill the water came upon her. She was found clinging to a tree, and after many attempts the train men rescued her. Mrs. Byrne, and her two daughters, who were drowned, were the mother and sisters of I. I. Byrne, Clerk of the Menifee County Court, and only recently moved there from near Cinnati. The rain fell with such volume and violence as to crush men to the earth. It was fortunate that no wind accompanied the storm.

UNEARTHED IN ALABAMA.
A Conspiracy to Murder the Whites in Choctaw County-The Ringleaders Arrested-The Most Desperate of them Tried by the Community and Lynched.
MOBILE, August 21.—In Choctaw county, Alabama, on Tuesday, the 15th inst., a bundle of papers, disclosing a well organized plan among the negroes to kill the entire white population of that county, was found near one of their rendezvous by two gentlemen. The matter was laid before the Solicitor. On Wednesday, the 16th, a quiet meeting of citizens of Mount Sterling and Butler was called at Butler to consider the best mode of suppressing the intended outbreak and massacre. After discussion it was agreed that the following ringleaders, Jack Turner, F. D. Barney, Jesse Wilson, Peter Hill, Willis Lyman, Aaron Scott and Range West, to whom had been assigned the duties of leading squads to Butler, Mt. Sterling, DeSotoville and other places, and killing all the whites at each place, should be arrested and lodged in jail.

Their arrest was effected on Thursday, the 17th, without disturbance or bloodshed. The same day a mass meeting of citizens of all classes was called for Saturday to decide the fate of the prisoners. The plot has been in existence since 1878, and the conspirators now number four hundred. They have powder, shot and guns. They think themselves sufficiently strong to accomplish their fiendish design. Sunday night, the 17th of September, had been appointed as the date for its consummation. The papers further showed that this day was selected because then the white people would be at camp-meeting unarmed, and could then offer no resistance.

The meeting called for Saturday brought together about 700 persons, among whom were about 150 negroes, who, after having the papers read, by an almost unanimous vote decided that Jack Turner was a turbulent and dangerous character, a regular firebrand in the community, and that the public demanded his immediate death. THE SHAM CONSPIRACY CASE.
We see that the New York Tribune is as skeptical as ourselves as to the alleged Alabama negro conspiracy which was recently made the pretext for lynching a prominent colored man in that State. The more we reflect upon the story the more convinced do we become that there is not a word of truth in the statement given to the public. The strong presumption is that it really means a revival of the villainous system of force and intimidation which disgraced the South for so many years. Nobody who knows anything about the negro will believe that he is capable of conspiracy after this fashion. His character is in all respects averse from operations of the kind. If he would conspire a little more he would get on better at the South, but he allows himself to be controlled by white men who are too often vulgar demagogues. In the case under notice we have little doubt that when the truth comes out it will appear that the man who was hanged had been an influential negro politician, and that his influence was interfering with that of some of the whisky-sodden blackguards who think the country belongs to them. We believe that all the conspiracy was on the side of these fellows, and that they have in fact established a terrorism over the colored people, and intend to use it for political effect. We trust, however, that the Tribune and other Eastern journals will at once dispatch trustworthy correspondents to the scene of action, and bring out all the facts. Certainly it will not do to accept the cock-and-bull story of a negro plot which the murderers have put forward to screen themselves.

THE CHOCTAW HANGING.
An Alabama Colored Man on the Infamous Outrage.
To the Editor of THE REPUBLICAN:

Seeing in the papers of the 22d instant a telegram from Mobile, Ala., dated August 21, in which it is stated that in Choctaw County, in that State, a bundle of papers was found on Tuesday, the 15th, disclosing a well organized plot by the negroes to kill the entire white population of the county, naming as ringleaders Jack Turner, F. D. Barney, Jesse Wilson, Peter Hill, Willis Lyman, Aaron Scott, and Range West, all of whom were arrested and imprisoned, and that it was decided by an almost unanimous vote of 700, 150 of whom were negroes present on the occasion, that Jack Turner was a turbulent fellow and a firebrand of the community, and that the public demanded his death, upon which decision the said Jack Turner was hung, please allow me sufficient space in the columns of your paper to express my opinion of the transaction and the cause which induced it. In the first place I do not believe that the

NEGROES IN THE COUNTY OF CHOCTAW, or any other county in the State of Alabama, or any other State, are so vindictive or foolish as to enter into any such plot as the one named in the dispatch, to kill off the white people. On the contrary, I believe the story to have been put in circulation by the mob as an extenuation in the eyes of the public of the crime of the "deep damnation of the taking off" of Jack Turner, who doubtless was an active Republican at the recent election in that State, and as such was looked upon as "a dangerous character, a turbulent fellow, and a firebrand in the community," for which he was adjudged deserving of death. The public manner in which he was murdered had for its object the intimidation of other "dangerous char-
COURAGE TO OPPOSE THE BOURBONS
in the congressional elections to take place this fall in the State of Alabama, and to disgust the independent whites in that State with their colored allies, and to force them to abandon the Independent party and to act, as heretofore, with the regular Democracy. The time has passed when negroes had a sufficient incentive to kill off communities of white people. There was a time when they could have destroyed nearly the entire white population of the South with impunity had they desired to have done so. That time was during the rebellion, when all of the able-bodied white men were away from their homes fighting to rivet the chains of slavery more firmly upon their bondmen, having left behind them, in the care of these "dangerous fellows," their aged fathers, mothers, wives, and little ones.

DID THESE "DANGEROUS FELLOWS," in a single instance betray the trust reposed in them during those trying days to the South? No, a thousand times no! On the contrary, these "dangerous fellows" labored faithfully on the farms for the support of their masters at the front and the maintenance of their helpless families at home, caring for the latter with an affectionate fidelity unparalleled in the history of any people ever held in bondage with the near prospect of freedom before them. I ask, now that we are free, what is our reward for our fidelity to our former masters during the darkest period of their history. The answer to this question is not very creditable to the white people of the South.

FREED BY THE POWER OF THE UNITED STATES, the best efforts of our late masters have been brought into requisition to prevent our enjoyment of the fruits of freedom. Laws enacted granting us the ballot for protection are nullified for the purpose of keeping us by local enactments in a condition as abject as slavery itself. In proof of this, look at the penal laws of most of the Southern States enacted by the Democratic legislatures since their usurpation of power in those States. These laws are a disgrace to the age and country in which we live.

AS A CAPSTONE TO THIS SUPERSTRUCTURE of infamy they now upon trumped up pretexts hang us up without mercy, and proclaim to the world that we are "dangerous, turbulent fellows, firebrands in the community," and therefore nothing but our removal by death can calm the fears of the public. Against all such outrageous proceedings as stated to have occurred in Choctaw County, as a colored man I most emphatically protest, and will continue to do so as often as they may happen, and as long as I can use my tongue or am able to put pen to paper.

Wm. V. TURNER.

Since writing the above I learn that there will be a meeting of the leading colored Republicans of Alabama residing in this city at 1510 L street northwest, on Saturday evening next, at 8 o'clock, for the purpose of taking action upon the Choctaw outrage.

W. V. T.

A FIENDISH PLOT. Discovery of a Devilish Scheme of Negroes to Murder the Whites—The Leader Hung.
MERIDIAN, August 21.—One of the most horrible and cruel conspiracies ever entered into by the negroes of this section, came to light in Choctaw county, Alabama, just across our State line, near Butler, the county seat, on Wednesday, of last week. It seems that some white men were riding along the road leading to Allee's mill, near DeSotoville, and found some papers, which, upon examination, proved to be the minutes of a negro organization, formed for

BRUTAL DEEDS OF BLOOD.

Information was gleaned from the minutes found that it was the intention of the negroes to make a general assault upon the whites between the fifteenth and seventeenth of October, and that the organization was four hundred strong and four years old, having been called into existence in 1878. Every member had subscribed to the most solemn oath, and binding obligation to secrecy, and the conspirators were pledged to kill every white man, woman and child in the county, "from the cradle to the grave."

A notoriously bad negro by the name of Jack Turner who, in his communications to the organization, signed himself "Gen. Jack Turner," was the evil spirit of whom the conspiracy was born, and who, if his wicked scheme proved successful, was to be made the ruler of the county with a big salary. There were also communications from "Capt. Jessie Wilson" and "Capt. Peter Hill" among the papers.

THE PLAN WAS,
when the time came for action, to divide the organization into three companies, to be commanded by "General Jack Turner," "Capt. Jessie Wilson" and "Capt. Peter Hill," who were to take up positions in the Butler, Mt. Sterling and DeSotoville neighborhoods, and attack the whole county simultaneously, and slaughter every man, woman and child that wore a white skin.

This news was circulated rapidly over the county among the white people, who organized and armed themselves and went in search of the blacks who were planning to slaughter them. They soon came upon "Gen. Jack Turner," "Cap. Jessie Wilson," "Captain Peter Hill," Secretary Fred. Bouner, Limon, a preacher, and two other leaders, names unknown, and took them in custody to Butler, the county seat, where they were lodged in jail.

Saturday morning Secretary Bonner was taken from the jail by the whites and interrogated, and notwithstanding the proof was coulusive against him, he denied acknowledge of the conspiracy and affirmed with Christian-like sincerity his innocence. He was

TIED UP BY THE TOES,
while Rev. Limon was brought out

to tell what he knew. He didn't know anything at first, but under the refreshing and persuasive influence of the lash, applied vigorously to his bared back, he remembered and told a great many things.

When the minutes were read to him, he admitted that he had heard them read twice before in the meeting; that he knew the conspiracy existed; that it was the intention of the negroes to kill the people, take possession of the county and make General Jack Turner rules, but that he had nothing to do with it. He admitted that he had been carrying the call around and getting the negroes to join, and that when arrested he was on his last round, and that he was paid fifty cents a day for his services. He could not be whipped into telling where the books and other papers of the organization were kept. He denied all knowledge of their whereabouts; said he knew they existed, but did not know where they were kept. He said that one of the negroes asked in the jail the night before if the white people had found the books and other papers, and that Jack Turner spoke up and said:

"No, they are not quite that d—d smart."

After this admission and other conclusive proofs against him, it was unanimously agreed among the whites that "Gen. Jack Turner ought to swing." So accordingly he was taken from the jail, and between the hours of twelve and one o'clock in the broad open day light of the day he was

HANGED TO THE LIMB OF A TREE on the main street of the town.

There was a strong intimation manifested on the part of the people to hang the other six, but older and cooler counsel prevailed, and they were spared.

It is said the people were as quiet and cool as people well could be under the circumstances, and that the execution of Turner was as deliberate as if done under the forms of law.

All is quiet now, and no further trouble is likely to occur.

The following preamble and resolutions were adopted at a meeting of the Arthur Republican Club, in Mobile, Friday evening, August 25th, 1882.

Whereas, information having reached us of the unlawful arrest, inhuman beating of a large number of our colored republican brethren, and of the diabolical and cold blooded murder of Jack Turner, a leading colored republican at Butler, Choctaw county, in this State at midday of the 19th inst, by the so-called citizens of Choctaw county.

We, the members of the Arthur-Republican Club of the Port of Mobile in meeting assembled do hereby denounce such outrageous blood-thirsty and inhuman proceedings as those perpetrated upon the late Jack Turner, and his fellow republicans of Choctaw county, as defiant to the laws of the State of Alabama, and an infringement of the rights and liberties of our colored brethren under the laws and constitution of the United States.

Having received the account given by one of the murderers, as published in and endorsed by the leading democratic paper of the State, the Montgomery Advertiser, of the unfounded rumor to injure and harm the white people of Choctaw county, we hereby denounce the entire so-called insurrection as fabulous and devoid of any truth. We further denounce the murderers of the late Jack Turner as fakers of the truth, and their inhuman and brutal conduct, without a paralleled in the history of our country. The Montgomery (Ala.) Advertiser is a "regular organization" Democratic paper. It has never wavered in its allegiance to the Bourbon Democracy. It is good authority for Alabama news. Then follows the above quotation describing the torture inflicted on negroes to make them "squeal." All the captains were "scourged" and one "terribly tortured." He refused to "squeal." It is possible he knew nothing to "squeal."

It is no excuse to say they conspired to perpetrate a great crime. There is but one way to find that out in a country of law.

Governor Cobb, of Alabama, Denounces the Choctaw Outrage.

The following letter from the Governor of Alabama, by his private secretary, is a sufficient answer to the efforts of Northern Democratic editors to make light of the hanging of Jack Turner, at Butler, Choctaw County, Ala., on the 19th ult. It is addressed to the State's attorney for the circuit:

MONTGOMERY, Aug. 30, 1882.

Hon. George W. Taylor, Butler, Ala.:

DEAR SIR: The death of the negro Jack Turner at the hands of a mob in Choctaw County, the circumstances under which the lawless act was perpetrated, and the use that is being made of the affair, constitute an event of such gravity that the governor deems it important to have from the officers of the county charged therein with the enforcement of the law and the maintenance of the peace a full report of all the facts in the case. No other recent event in the State has occasioned so much regret at home or has elsewhere excited so profound a feeling. The peace and dignity of the State are offended, the good name of the Commonwealth suffers abroad, and the county is reproached wherever the story is told. The law provides adequate punishment for every criminal act and establishes all the necessary agencies for the administration of justice. Mob violence is lawlessness to be deplored by every good citizen and to be resisted by every conservator of the peace. The act under consideration, notwithstanding the provocation unofficially reported, appears to be an aggravated one, for the victim was in the hands of the officers of justice, and in jail would have been as powerless for the prosecution of the plans attributed to him as he is in the grave. He was murdered, and under circumstances that afford mendacious enemies of our people and section a pretext for attributing his death to political or race antipathies. The governor understands, of course, that your official duties in such cases begin with the grand jury and end with the petit jury, and he knows you will fearlessly and faithfully discharge them; but he hopes in the meantime, and promptly, you will take it upon yourself, asking the assistance of the county officers, to make a full investigation of the tragedy and report the facts to him. Very respectfully,

ROBERT McKEE,
Private Secretary.

The reply to this is addressed to the governor, and makes more than a column in the Montgomery Advertiser. It is addressed to the governor and begins with the words: "In response to your letter." Moody, tax assessor; Joseph Breitling, county commissioner; J. C. Chapman, clerk circuit court; and S. P. Smith, county treasurer. It is a defense of the sickening atrocity, and merely claims that the murdered man was dangerous. We quote the following:

Under the firm belief of imperious and impending necessity, they (the people) took the law into their own hands, and, as they believed, to save the lives of many, they sacrificed one.

They disdain to answer the governor's argument that the victim Turner, being in jail, was as powerless for harm "as he is in the grave;" but they show how deep his rebuke cuts into their sensibilities in the words with which they close. They say:

Just for decency's sake, and in order to seem to be divided on the subject, some of the Democratic papers ought to take sides with Alabama's Democratic governor against the Choctaw County mob murderers.

The Murdered Deputy Collector.
DETAILS OF THE KILLING OF JAMES M. DAVIS BY MOONSHINERS IN TENNESSEE.

Deputy Collector James M. Davis, of the internal revenue service, who was waylaid and murdered by moonshiners near Nashville, Tenn., a few days ago, was one of the most valuable men in the service. The commissioner of internal revenue says he never hesitated to do his duty, no matter what the odds, and that he was as brave as a lion. He has long been a terror to moonshiners, and they have been trying hard to get him out of the way. About a year ago he had his hip broken and his skull fractured in two places. Commissioner Raum ordered him here at once, and he was under the care of Dr. Bliss for some time. He entirely recovered from his injuries, and since has done good work. His assassination is quite a blow to the internal revenue service. Although Commissioner Raum is anxious to bring the assassins to justice, it is generally believed in Tennessee that the reward of $300 for each is insufficient to secure their arrest, as all are regarded as desperate men, well used to handling firearms.

A gentleman, who arrived at Nashville from the mountains a few days ago, said that if Davis had had half a chance he would singly and alone have fought his assassins, eight to twelve in number; was riding without a saddle girth, which had been lost, so that when the horse jumped at the first fire he was thrown to the ground. He lay on the earth as if dead for a short time, having been hit in the leg. He finally got up and started back limping, when the bushwhackers began to fire at him and he again fell prostrate. One of the assassins then walked up upon the embankment and shot the top of his head off with a double-barrelled shotgun. Davis and his prisoner. Vickers, were allowed to pass the ambuscade before the murderers fired upon him. It was thought that this was done in order to get Vickers out of range of their shots. Davis, wounded as he was, fired three shots, while U. S. Commissioner Campbell, who was 150 yards behind, fired one shot. After they had killed Davis the party departed, taking a path leading over Ben Lomond Mountain, above McMinnville, whence they came. They were seen in the suburbs of McMinnville on the morning preceding the assassination and some persons talking to them. One hundred shots were fired. Twenty-six bullet holes were found in the back portion of Davis' coat.

Deputy Collector Davis and his men were returning from Beersheba Springs to this place Monday last, and when about three miles from here Davis was fired upon by some parties in ambush. At the first fire Thomas Vickers, who was riding with Davis, fled. When shot Davis fell from his horse, but soon regained his feet and started back up the road toward Campbell and Cathcart who were in the rear. He had not gone far, however, when he was fired upon again and killed. An inquest was held and the body was brought to town. Between twenty and thirty bullets were found in the body and the skull was litterally shattered with pistol balls.

The shooting was done by men concealed behind breastworks constructed of logs and cord-wood and covered over with cedar brush. This structure was about ten feet from the Beersheba road and the underbrush had been cut away so as to leave an unobstructed view. The assaulting party is estimated at from 10 to 15 men, George Campbell, who has been with Davis a long time, and was with him on this trip, states that Davis' conduct was very strange for two or three days prior to his death, that he manifested signs of restlessness and depression altogether unusual in him. DAVIS' DEATH.
A Presentiment Which Made Him Restive.
It appears that Davis had a presentiment that he would be killed before he got off the mountains. In consequence he was restive from the time he left McMinnville. When he had reached a point not far from the ambuseade on the Beersheba road, Vickers says Davis called his attention to some loose horses on Ben Lomond mountain, but Vickers could not observe them. Davis had been to Beersheba and was on his way to McMinnville. His assassins had come over the point at Ben Lomond mountain. At one place on the mountain the road to the rear could be observed for a distance of two miles. When Davis and his men came in sight, on this part of the road, a pistol shot was fired. This was believed to have been a signal to the assassins that Davis and his men had come in sight, and for them to make all the necessary arrangements to kill him. The shooting did not occur until half an hour after the signal. Before reaching the ambuseade Davis got Vickers to get down and let out his stirrup straps, that he might simply touch the stirrups with his toes. The ambush was so constructed that each one of the eight men had a porthole through which he could fire, the base of it being a large log, with wings, made of cord wood, thrown out in front and on each side, and covered with cedar. It is believed the oysters, in the cans found, must have been eaten on some day previous to the assassination. It is said that in their testimony before the coroner's jury, two wood-choppers within fifteen feet of whom the assassins passed, denied having known the men. The white man testified that he thought he knew five of the men when they were approaching him, but he was satisfied he did not know any of them after they had passed by him. The negro testified that he did not know any of the men in the crowd and could not identify any one of them. They came upon him and his white companion so unexpectedly that he was scared and said to them out of fear, perhaps, more than anything else, "we surrender," supposing they had come after them, but why he could not tell. None of the men said anything, and went off in another direction.

It is thought that the two wood choppers, even if they had recognized any of the men, would not dare to say so from fear of the vengeance of the assassins or their friends. It will thus be very difficult to discover the men who killed Davis.

Some men are suspected of having taken part in the assassination, but it is doubtless whether the real assassins will ever be found.—[American.

The Richmond State of the 29th contains an account of the killing of a negro in Moore county by a member of a sheriff's posse. The details are as follows. The homicide took place in the county, jail, where the prisoner, Willis Edwards, a stout negro man about twenty-five years of age, was confined on a peace warrant. He became desperate because the sheriff informed him that he would have to remain in jail until court time. He raved and swore in an outrageous manner, tore planks from the ceiling with his bare hands and told the sheriff that if he could get at him he would kill him. The sheriff reported to a magistrate that Edwards was desperate and would soon break out of jail. The magistrate told him to take the prisoner out of the cell and chain him in the dungeon till he became quiet. A posse were summoned for that purpose and its members were increased as the desperate disposition of the man became more apparent. In the meantime a large crowd had gathered in the corridors of the jail. Edwards denied the crowd, cursing them, said he would kill the first man that laid hands upon him, that he would kill somebody if he ever got out, anyway, and told the sheriff he might as well get his rope ready to hang him. An attempt was made to take him, when he rushed into the corridors, swinging a piece of plank right and left among the crowd, but in the struggle he finally got into the cell again, carrying Mr. Berry Birford with him. He struck the gentleman two on three severe blows with the piece of scantling, and was preparing to strike him again when Mr. Binford shot him twice in the back, and right arm, upon which he fell. Willis also broke the fingers of a Mr. Robert Simpson in the affray. The negro lived one hour after the shooting, and a post-mortem examination showed that one ball passed through the kidneys, the second through the liver, and the fourth shattered the bone in the right arm. It is thought this shot was fired by some other party, as the ball was smaller than those from Mr. Binford's pistol, which were of a thirty-two calibre. The coroner's jury rendered a verdict that the negro Willis Edwards came to his death by pistol shots fired by B. H. Binford in self-defence, and that the shooting was justifiable. Mr. Binford's injuries were quite severe. He suffered from two severe blows, one on the neck, and the other on the shoulder. The blow delivered on the neck was a slanting one, otherwise it would have killed him instantly.

Just at the close of the last term of our Superior Court, Wilson Edwards, colored, of Sandy Ridge Township, was lodged in jail, for want of bondsmen, a peace warrant having been sworn out against him by a colored woman whom he had endeavored to shoot.

On Wednesday, when his dinner was sent up, he was found lying on the floor of his cell, without coat or shirt on, and sullenly refused to take his dinner. In an hour afterward, Sheriff Price went up and found him still lying on the floor, in a sullen mood, and in reply to the question as to why he didn't eat his dinner, used profane and abusive language. From this and other matters, Sheriff Price thought perhaps his mind was wrong, and that he had better be ironed before hurting himself or some one else. He sent off and procured the help of three or four stout colored men, but upon their arrival he was found to be in the notion of fighting, and threatened to kill any one who entered the cell; and being well armed with heavy stuff torn from the ceiling of his cell, he was rightly considered a dangerous customer. By this time, other help came, among them several white men—J. E. W. Austin, Jno. S. Richardson, B. H. Binford, E. T. wade, Rob't Simpson, and others—and as it was dangerous to go into the room where he was, he having all advantages, it was decided that it was best to open the door and allow him to come out, and overpower him, as he came. But it was found that he was harder to manage than they had anticipated, and he came so quick, with a stick in each hand, and his naked body so slick he could not be held, that he took the crowd somewhat by surprise, and began striking right and left with his murderous weapons. Ben. Blakeney, colored, was the first victim, he having been punched in the mouth with a stick, before the door was opened. Rob't Simpson next had two fingers broken. Berry H. Binford was next struck about the neck, and from this the negro's spite seemed to centre on Binford, and he followed him on across the passage into an opposite dungeon, where he "got in" another blow, which brought Mr. B. to the wall. Just here, three shots were fired, and though they entered the negro's body and two of them produced fatal wounds, he struggled on until forced to the floor by J. Richardson, who had swung to a handkerchief the negro had around his neck. After he was down, it was known that he was seriously hurt, and physicians were sent for, and Dr. Welsh soon came and said there was no chance to save him. In the meantime, Mr. Binford was taken to a room below and Dr. Ramsay called in, who found his patient badly hurt and suffering greatly from the blow on the side of the neck and shoulder. Had this blow been otherwise than a glancing one, Binford would, in all probability, have been instantly killed.

The negro died in less than an hour—one ball having passed through the liver, a second just above, while a third went through the kidney.

Afterwards, a former fellow-prisoner who was taken from the cell only a few days ago, told Sheriff Price that the prisoner, Edwards, had disclosed to him a plan he had formed to escape, which was to "play off crazy," and should Sheriff A. J. Price come alone and open the door he would brain him and rush out. Should the Sheriff come with help he would fight his way through and escape or be killed in the attempt. He was a powerful, well muscled, able-bodied negro 30 or 35 years old, and was known as a desperate character. The affair of course is to be greatly regretted but no blame can be attached to any one, as it was necessary to iron him if possible or he would have torn up the jail and come out, and after the effort was made it became necessary to fire on him or he would have killed others.

Since Edwards had been jailed, conclusive evidence has been brought out, showing that he was the person who shot Jack Huneycutt, col'd, some time ago, in Sandy Ridge Township, mention of which was made in this paper at the time.

A TEST FOR INSANITY.—Dr. Lamson will not have died in vain if the suggestion made by one of the British authorities on insanity is hereafter applied to test the perceptive faculties of alleged insane murderers. The suggestion is that a red hot poker be handed to the said alleged insane person; if he takes it, he is to be adjudged as really unable to distinguish between right and wrong; but if he refuses it, then he is to he considered as responsible and be made to suffer accordingly. The test is a very simple one, and there seems to be no reason why it should not be accepted as satisfactory. He who can remember that a red hot poker burns can also remember to kill another is a crime.—London Graphic.

Kansas City, April 3.—The news of the killing of Jesse James created an immense sensation in this city, although the report was generally treated with discredit and even at this late hour many unbelievers can be found. This afternoon as soon as the news was received here Police Commissioner Craig left for St. Joseph with a heavily armed posse of men to guard the body of James and furnish protection for the man who killed him. At the station house it was learned that a young man who has been hanging about the station for several weeks past, was the person who shot and killed Jesse James. Ford left this city about a week since and joined James in the vicinity of St. Joseph, remaining with him until an opportunity to kill him was found. From the police it is learned that Ford, who is said to be a member of the gang, was under control of Craig, and has been used as an instrument for James' destruction. Ford is a young man about twenty-two years of age, and looked like a verdant from the country. In appearance he is a mere boy, and is the last person in the world to be taken for the slayer of an outlaw. The Oregon Short Line. Omaha, Neb., April 3.—The report is telegraphed from Sioux City that the Union Pacific had determined to abandon all work on the Oregon Short Line is without any foundation whatever. Assistant General Manager Kemball, of the Union Pacific, says that every nerve is being strained to push the Oregon Short Line as rapidly as possible. The track has been laid within eight miles of Snake river, Montana. The bridge across Snake river will be in position in a few weeks, and a large grading force will soon commence work on the west side of the Snake river and from there to Wood river and Boise City, Idaho, work will be rapidly rushed forward. Steel rails have been contracted for and are being rooled and shipped to the front. It is expected this season to grade to Boise City and to lay between three and four hundred miles of track. Riotous Negroes.
St. Louis, Mo., April 3.—A Republican's Rockport, Mo., special says: Some twenty or more drunken negroes created a disturbance on the street last night, and assaulted one or two white men. Several special deputies were sworn in to maintain order, who notified the negroes that they must disperse or be arrested. One of them attempted to strike one of the officers, who drew a weapon and fired at his assailant without hitting him. The negroes then fled, but some were taken, and while some fifteen or twenty men and boys were standing on the street talking together a volley from guns and pistols was fired at them by negroes from an alley on the opposite side of the street, and one of them wounded, but none seriously. Great excitement ensued, and ten of the negroes were arrested and locked up.

Killing of a Bad Man.

Nashville, Tenn., April 3.—An American's Murfreesboro special says: O'Brien, a special deputy sheriff, went out last night to arrest Bethel Thompson, who shot an officer in Shelbyville last year when about to be arrested for horse stealing. Thompson was concealing himself at a house of ill-fame and was found in bed. While O'Brien was reading his warrant Thompson shot him with a pistol which he drew from under his pillow, the bullet passing through the neck, inflicting a bad and probably fata' wound. O'Brien returned the fire, killing Thompson instantly. Thompson was the third man O'Brien has killed.

Stabbed by a Companion.

St. Louis, April 3.—A special to the Republican says: While Charles Fisher and a man named Trotter were riding side by side on horse-back near Poplin station, on the Cairo branch of the Iron Mountain railway, yesterday afternoon, they got into yn altercation about some business transaction, and Trotter drew a knife and stabbed Fisher to the heart, killing him. Trotter was arrested. There was great excitement and threats of lynching him were freely made by Fisher's friends.

St. Paul and Winnipeg dispatches record heavy snow storms along the Canadian Pacific, which block traveling until warm weather. The storm at Winnipeg was unprecedentedly severe. J. W. Kerr, until recently paying teller of the Bank of the Republic, Washington, killed himself on the 29th. He left a note, saying: "Realizing that I have expended money belonging to others to an extent that I can never repay, I have sought this relief from dishonor, sorrow and disgrace."

JOHN KENNEDY and John O'Neal, carpenters, fell from a scaffolding in Denver, Colo., March 30, and were precipitated a distance of seventy-five feet. Kennedy will probably recover. O'Neal is a native of Prince Edward Island, where he has a wife. He will probably die from his injuries.

During a fire which destroyed several frame buildings in Le Sueur, Minn., on the 30th, Miss Fishbaum was burned to death, and another girl was slightly hurt by jumping from a window.

EX-GOVERNOR MOSES, of South Carolina, has again been arrested in New York on a charge of swindling.

ALLEN Fox, a wealthy citizen of Louisville, Ky., aged 81 years, mortally wounded himself with a razor the other evening.

TRUMAN DUNHAM, President of the Cleveland Linseed Oil Works, an old and honored citizen, was caught in machinery, March 30, and killed. He was alone in the basement, where there was a large belt which runs the grinder; in some unknown way he was caught in the belt, carried into the machinery and the body shockingly crushed. Deceased had been trustee of the Cleveland water-works for many years.

J. W. SHEEHAN, a young man stopping at the Metropolitan Hotel, Kansas City, Mo., was found dead in his room, March 30, having taken poison. The following note was found on the table: "My father's address is William Sheehan, North Walpole, N. H." Sheehan had a letter of recommendation from the Smith Refrigerator Manufacturing Company, of Michigan City, Ind., speaking of him as a sober, industrious man. It is supposed he took the dose in a fit of despondency, finding himself out of work and among strangers.

Two inmates of the Dayton (Ohio) Lunatic Asylum had a deadly struggle the other night. One, named John Drummond, had arrived that day. He was a farmer, living in Brown county, and the cause of his insanity was said to be jealousy. He had several times attempted suicide, and threatened to kill others. On his arrival he was quiet and tractable, but during the night he became noisy and was removed to a strong cell, in which was an old man named O'Connell, of quiet habit. When the watchman entered the cell, toward morning, O'Connell bounded out from the corner; frantic with excitement. He said Drummond had attacked and bitten him, so he choked him quiet. Drummond was found dead on the floor covered with blood, one eye gouged out and otherwise terribly mutilated. O'Connell was also badly bruised and scratched in many places, and one finger was nearly bitten off.

At Rocheport, Mo., April 1st, Jos. Mitchell, colored, insulted Marion Wyatt, white, who is as quiet and peaceable a man as can be found. A few words were passed, and on Mitchell attempting to strike Wyatt he knocked him down. General Wilhite, backed by several other negroes, sided with Mitchell, and Wyatt drew a revolzer to protect himself. The blacks then left the place and gathered to the number of twenty-five in the street opposite the Post-office, making considerable disturbance. A number of special deputies were sworn in and went to the crowd and told them they must scatter or be arrested, Some left, but Wm. Barber tried to strike Thos. White, an officer, who, in self-defence, shot at him twice, but in the darkness missed him. An exchange threatens his delinquent subscribers after this fashion:

Now we have got 'em. It says: "A new postal law or decision authorizes the publishers of newspapers to arrest any man as a thief who takes his paper and refuses to pay for. The reaper and mower trade is dull in Richmond, for the reason that our dealers have sold out all the stock they had on hand. The demand was large.

The brick work on Jo. Sanderson's new business house is progressing finely, and if the workmen could have suitable weather, it would soon be finished.

Harvesters are making things rattle this week between showers. If we could only have a week of settled weather the wheat would all be nicely cut and shocked and some of it stacked.

Rev. Dr. Flack, of Excelsior, was in the city on Friday night last. He is a very pleasant gentleman and by his energy and zeal has built up a considerable town at Excelsior.

Mr. Jas. A. Tuttle has sold his saddle and harness shop in this city to Mr. Hudgins, who will continue the business at the old stand on west side of the square. If he advertises his business well he will make money.

Uncle Billy Griffey was in town yesterday and called in. He says he thinks of running for State Senator on the U. T. P. tickets, and proposes to give the boys a lively hustle. He wants the DEMOCRAT to draw it mild on him, and of course we will.

Dr. J. D. Taylor and family, who left here some months ago, to make their home in Chillicothe, we learn will return at once and locate permanently in Richmond again. After all they find there is no place like home. We gladly welcome them to our midst once more.

Mr. Thomas Holt has sold his interest in the store of Holt & Woodson, under this office, to his partner, Harry Woodson, who will conduct the business in the future at the old stand. He will keep a full stock at all times and do you right. Don't forget the place.

Prof. B. F. Duncan, who has occupied the responsible position of President of Richmond College in this city for three years, has been elected to the position of principal of the public schools at Gallatin, Daviess county. While we regret very much losing Prof. Duncan from Richmond, we rejoice that he is called to so pleasant a town as Gallatin. He is a worthy gentleman an earnest christian, a good citizen and one among the best educationalists that has ever dwelt among us, and he will reflect honor on any community in which he may dwell. The good people of Gallatin can rest assured that they have drawn a prize, in securing the services of Prof. Duncan, and they should give him that earnest support necessary to make his work complete. He has the best wishes of the editor of this paper for his future success and prosperity.
